core: testing a claim against textual evidence

claims.claim: Close reading attends carefully to textual details and formal features in order to develop an interpretation rather than merely summarize a text.
Textual analysis examines parts of a text to explain meaning and can support more than one reading when the evidence is reasoned.
Analytical claims should be supported with textual evidence and explanation rather than preference alone.
Rereading, selective annotation, and attention to recurring language, images, and structure can support critical analysis.
Close reading is not a license to substitute biographical or contextual claims for evidence from the passage; background can inform a broader analysis but the method foregrounds the text.
A responsible interpretation may be revised when other relevant details complicate the initial claim.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Some course materials use close reading, critical reading, textual analysis, and literary analysis with overlapping rather than identical meanings.
positions: Pima Writing II calls close reading or critical reading an active reading practice used to support an argument about meaning.
OpenStax describes textual analysis more broadly as examining a text's parts to explain meaning.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson treats close reading as a focused evidence-based practice within the broader work of textual analysis and avoids claiming the terms are universally interchangeable.

unsupportedExistingClaims: The generated draft defined close reading only as a generic foundational concept and supplied no verified account of its evidence-based method, limits, or relation to summary.
